inputs.question: In primary health care, does using mobile phones or tablets to keep track of the care each patient gets, together with on-screen prompts that guide health workers, reminder messages sent to patients, or both, improve the care people receive and their health?
inputs.scope:
Covers: Primary health care settings where health workers use mobile devices (phones or tablets) to digitally track individual clients' health status and services received. This is combined with either on-screen decision support for health workers, targeted communication to clients (such as SMS reminders), or both. It covers effects on care delivery (adherence to recommended practice, service coverage and timeliness), on patient health outcomes, and any reported unintended consequences, compared with usual paper-based or non-digital care.
Out of scope:
- Whether stand-alone SMS reminders to patients, without health-worker tracking, improve adherence or attendance (That is a different intervention, client communication alone, with its own separate body of evidence. The question is about tracking combined with prompts or reminders.)
- Effectiveness of telemedicine or remote consultations between patients and clinicians (Telemedicine delivers care at a distance. It is not about tracking clients and prompting health workers during routine care.)
- Hospital electronic health records and inpatient clinical decision support systems (The question is restricted to primary health care settings, and hospital systems differ in users, infrastructure and outcomes.)
- Cost-effectiveness and implementation feasibility (connectivity, device maintenance, health worker acceptability) (These matter for scaling, but they are separate from whether the intervention improves care and health, and they need economic and qualitative evidence.)
- Consumer health apps used by patients on their own for self-management (The question concerns tools used by health workers to track clients, not self-directed patient apps.)
inputs.judgement: Digital tracking may improve primary care workers' ability to follow recommended antenatal and chronic disease practices, quality of patient records, patient health outcomes and service use.

This is combined with either on-screen decision support for health workers, targeted communication to clients (such as SMS reminders), or both. It covers effects on care delivery (adherence to recommended practice, service coverage and timeliness), on patient health outcomes, and any reported unintended consequences, compared with usual paper-based or non-digital care.
Out of scope:
- Whether stand-alone SMS reminders to patients, without health-worker tracking, improve adherence or attendance (That is a different intervention, client communication alone, with its own separate body of evidence. The question is about tracking combined with prompts or reminders.)
- Effectiveness of telemedicine or remote consultations between patients and clinicians (Telemedicine delivers care at a distance. It is not about tracking clients and prompting health workers during routine care.)
- Hospital electronic health records and inpatient clinical decision support systems (The question is restricted to primary health care settings, and hospital systems differ in users, infrastructure and outcomes.)
- Cost-effectiveness and implementation feasibility (connectivity, device maintenance, health worker acceptability) (These matter for scaling, but they are separate from whether the intervention improves care and health, and they need economic and qualitative evidence.)
- Consumer health apps used by patients on their own for self-management (The question concerns tools used by health workers to track clients, not self-directed patient apps.)
inputs.judgement: Programme planners should take these factors into account when designing and implementing programmes.
